subject: history_social
passage: In the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, watchmaking spread through the villages of the Jura Mountains in western Switzerland, where many farm families made watch parts at home and sold them to merchants who organized the trade. Historians often explain this spread by the region's thin, rocky soils, which made farming alone a poor living. Historian Lukas Meier argues that a different feature of the mountains mattered more: the long winters, when deep snow halted farm work for months and left families with time to fill.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly support Meier's argument?

choices.A: Families in the villages with the poorest soils earned the largest share of their yearly income from making watch parts.
choices.B: Watch parts made in Jura farmhouses were sold to merchants based in Geneva and other towns.
choices.C: Snowy villages took up watchmaking early even with good soils, while poor-soiled villages with mild winters took it up late.
choices.D: Many Jura watchmakers specialized in making a single kind of part, such as springs or small gears.

explanation.why: Meier contrasts two causes, winter idleness and poor soils, and says winters mattered more. Support must separate the two. Villages with long winters but good soils adopted watchmaking early, while villages with poor soils but mild winters adopted it late, so winter length, not soil, predicts the spread.
explanation.A: Incorrect. A link between poor soils and watchmaking income supports the usual explanation that Meier disputes, not his argument.
explanation.B: Incorrect. Where the parts were sold does not show why families took up the work.
explanation.C: Correct. Watchmaking followed winter length even when soil quality pointed the other way, which supports Meier over the usual explanation.
explanation.D: Incorrect. How the work was divided among workers says nothing about why watchmaking spread.
